title: Causal Epistemic Dynamics and Mechanism-Aware Hallucination Prevention in Large Language Models: A Theoretical Framework, Preregistered Protocol, and Pre-Confirmatory Validation
content: Large language models (LLMs) generate fluent statements that are unsupported by available evidence or inconsistent with established facts. Existing mitigations retrieval augmentation, uncertainty estimation, factuality evaluation, self-verification, and representation-level intervention typically treat hallucination as a single observable outcome rather than as the product of distinguishable computational and decision processes. This manuscript proposes a causal epistemic framework that represents factual knowledge availability, context-conditioned activation, information propagation, generation-policy decisions, external evidence, and factual outcomes as variables in a structural causal model. Four operational failure classes are specified knowledge deficiency, activation failure, propagation failure, and decision-policy failure as hypotheses about dominant causal pathways, not as mutually exclusive or directly observable categories. We derive a sufficient risk-reduction condition under imperfect mechanism classification, formulate total and interventional-mediation estimands, and specify a mechanism-aware intervention policy (CEMAP-LLM) with a conformal uncertainty-aware extension. The methodological contribution is a complete, preregistered experimental programme: verified data sources, a controlled association environment with known exposure, an eight-test negative-control acceptance battery, gated execution, and a full analysis-and-reporting contract for the protocol-empirical stratum, including estimands, cluster-bootstrap estimators, multiplicity control, evaluator-error correction, and explicit falsification conditions. No protocol-empirical result on language models is reported, and hypotheses H1–H3 remain untested. We report an executed pre-confirmatory record: deterministic corpus construction with preregistration locks, known-answer instrument validation, and a surrogate-model probe exhibiting a recognition–extraction dissociation. The intended contribution is a falsifiable, reproducible bridge from causal diagnosis to mechanism-specific hallucination prevention.
